title: Tramell Tillman Says ‘I Had to Sign NDAs’ Before Even Meeting for ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Role: ‘A Little Frustrating Because Everything Was Shrouded in Secrecy’
description:
Tramell Tillman is going to play a big role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s future. And he can finally talk about it. 

	Tillman, who won an Emmy
body:
Tramell Tillman is going to play a big role in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s future. And he can finally talk about it. 

	Tillman, who won an Emmy last year for his supporting role in Apple TV’s “Severance,” had been hoping to appear in a Marvel movie for some time, and heard from his team that Destin Daniel Cretton, the director of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” wanted to meet with him. But the meeting came with a catch: “I’m pretty sure I had to sign NDAs even before that conversation happened,” he tells GQ in a new interview.
	

	The actor found the mystery around his role — Bill Metzger, a comic-book character who opposes the X-Men and, in the MCU, will be a government official helping to mitigate the damage superheroes cause — to be challenging: “It was a little frustrating, because everything was shrouded in secrecy,” he tells GQ. “So I wasn’t even sure specifically how the character would fit into the world of the movie, and I’m pretty sure they had to play their cards very close to the chest because they weren’t sure if I was going to accept it.


	Along with Sadie Sink’s Jean Grey, Metzger is a crossover from the “X-Men” stories into “Spider-Man”; Marvel brass didn’t want the fact of these two worlds colliding onscreen to leak. But it presented a conundrum for an actor who didn’t know what part he might be signing up for. “So we’re kind of playing this back-and-forth game where I’m asking Destin, ‘Well, what can you tell me?,’” Tillman recalls. “And Destin would say, ‘It’s this and that, but I can’t say anything more than that.’ But he told me it was a pivotal role, and that’s about it. So this was a leap of faith. Do I want to jump at this opportunity or do I want to hold off and wait for another potential opportunity from Marvel?”
	

	Tillman decided to take the leap, and crafted a character he compares to Barack Obama: “I had this inkling that Metzger had just a little bit of swag, a little smoothness,” he says. “There’s a fullness, a calmness, a steadiness there.” And now that “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has become the second-fastest film to reach $1 billion in total box office gross, Tillman can likely expect to reprise the role — this time knowing what he’s signed up for.

schema.headline: Tramell Tillman Says ‘I Had to Sign NDAs’ Before Even Meeting for ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Role: ‘A Little Frustrating Because Everything Was Shrouded in Secrecy’

title: Netflix Shuts Down Studio Behind ‘Unhinged’ Game 6 Weeks After Release
description: Netflix is shutting down two studios, including the developer behind the David Fincher and Zach Cregger-backed horror game, “Unhinged,” which releas
body:
Netflix is shutting down two studios, including the developer behind the David Fincher and Zach Cregger-backed horror game, “Unhinged,” which released less than two months ago.

	The streaming service is closing “Unhinged” maker Night School Studio, which it acquired in 2021, and Moonloot, a Helsinki-based studio founded in 2022.

	“We are incredibly grateful to the talented colleagues we’re saying goodbye to today,” a Netflix spokesperson told Variety Thursday. “We thank them for all their contributions to Netflix, and wish them the best.”
	

	These new shutdowns are the latest in a series of moves that have whittled down Netflix’s internal game business, which now consists of Next Games, which is based in Helsinki, as well as a gaming team that works with external developers.

	Over the past few years, Netflix has divested studios Spry Fox (which was sold back to its founders last December), Boss Fight (which was shutdown last October after releasing a “Squid Game” mobile title for the streamer), and the AAA-focused Team Blue (which was shuttered in 2024).

	Under Netflix president of games Alain Tascan, who joined in his role at the end of 2024, Netflix’s gaming strategy is now focused on four key areas: kids (“Netflix Playground”), party (“Netflix Minigolf”), narrative (“Unhinged”) and mainstream (“FIFA World Cup: Launch Edition”). 

	Recently, Netflix has been expanding into games played on TVs using a phone as a controller, like “Unhinged” and “FIFA World Cup: Launch Edition.” Sources tell Variety the most internal excitement in the division surrounds monumentum for cloud games and kids games.
	

	News of the Night School Studio and Moonloot shutdowns was first reported by GameFile.

schema.headline: Netflix Shuts Down Studio Behind ‘Unhinged’ Game 6 Weeks After Release

title: WOW – Women Of Wrestling Sets Major Season 5 Expansion, Jeanie Buss to Appear On-Camera (EXCLUSIVE)
description: WOW – Women Of Wrestling is going through a major growth spurt for its fifth season — which includes the league’s first live broadcast and expanded
body:
WOW – Women Of Wrestling is going through a major growth spurt for its fifth season — which includes the league’s first live broadcast and expanded on-camera presence from Jeanie Buss.

	Season 5 will broadcast live from L.A. Live in downtown Los Angeles, anchoring WOW’s marquee events as part of a broader live strategy. Co-owner and promoter Jeanie Buss will take on an increased role on-camera as part of this season.


	“Season 5 is personal for me in a new way,” Buss, governor and minority owner of the Los Angeles Lakers, says. “I’m taking on a bigger, more visible role, and fans are going to see a side of WOW they haven’t seen before. I’ve spent my career fighting for women to be seen and respected in spaces that weren’t built for us, and WOW exists to give women that platform, in the ring and beyond. Women’s sports are having a real moment, and this season delivers on everything we’ve been building toward.” 
	

	Founded by David McLane, who also created Gorgeous Ladies of Wrestling, WOW is the only all-women’s wrestling league on TV. It has a 93% audience return season over season, and its social following has grown 96% since Season 1. The first four seasons aired in national syndication via Paramount Global Content Distribution.

	“Taking WOW live from L.A. LIVE changes everything about the experience. Bigger moments, bigger stars, and the energy of a live crowd that fans at home feel in real time,” he says. “And this is the start of something larger, an annual calendar of marquee events that makes WOW a destination, not just a show. I’ve spent years building this league into a platform for women who belong in the spotlight, and this is the stage they’ve always deserved.”
	

	Andrew Simon, General Manager of L.A. LIVE, adds, “Women Of Wrestling has established itself as one of the most distinctive and exciting brands in sports entertainment today, and we’re thrilled to welcome WOW to L.A. LIVE. Jeanie Buss and David McLane have created something truly special, a unique sports and entertainment property that combines athletic excellence, entertainment, and inspiring storytelling in a way that resonates with audiences of all ages. As a destination known for hosting premier live events, we’re proud to provide the stage for WOW’s continued growth and for an event that will bring tremendous energy and excitement to our campus.”

	Live and women’s sports are big for television right now: Netflix acquired the FIFA Women’s World Cup and set WWE Raw live, and the WNBA signed new rights deals with Disney/ESPN, Amazon and NBCUniversal.

schema.headline: WOW – Women Of Wrestling Sets Major Season 5 Expansion, Jeanie Buss to Appear On-Camera (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Season 3 Finale Hits 21 Million Viewers in Three Days
description: “House of the Dragon” concluded its third season on HBO on Sunday night, with the finale reaching 21 million viewers in its first three days of avai
body:
“House of the Dragon” concluded its third season on HBO on Sunday night, with the finale reaching 21 million viewers in its first three days of availability. More than 11 million of those viewers were in the U.S.

	That total comes from a combination of Nielsen’s measurement of linear viewers on the HBO cable channel plus Warner Bros. Discovery’s own tally of streams on HBO Max. It represents a mostly steady trajectory for the season, with a slight decrease of 2% from the Season 3 premiere’s 21.5 million viewers. (WBD did not disclose viewership totals for Episodes 2-7.)
	

	Overall, the season is averaging 34 million viewers per episode thus far, nearly matching Season 2’s 35 million-viewer average. According to HBO, this puts it among the HBO Max’s top three most-watched returning seasons ever. 


	Sunday also marked the seventh and final episode of “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness.” The sketch series, created by and starring Larry David, is averaging approximately 4 million viewers per episode in the U.S. 

	More to come…

schema.headline: ‘House of the Dragon’ Season 3 Finale Hits 21 Million Viewers in Three Days

title: Warner Bros. Discovery’s Gerhard Zeiler to Recieve Directorate Award at This Year’s International Emmys
description: Warner Bros. Discovery president of international Gerhard Zeiler has been tapped to receive the 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award. He joins
body:
Warner Bros. Discovery president of international Gerhard Zeiler has been tapped to receive the 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award. He joins Netflix chief content officer Bela Bajaria, who was previously announced as this year’s honoree for the org’s founders award. Zeiler and Bajaria will acceot their awards at the 54th International Emmy Awards Gala on Monday, Nov. 23, in New York.

	“Gerhard Zeiler has built and led some of the world’s most influential media businesses, helping shape the international television industry through periods of profound change,” said International Academy of Television Arts & Sciences president/CEO Bruce L. Paisner in a statement. “Throughout his career, his commercial acumen has been grounded in a deep appreciation for the creative talent and storytelling that define our business.”
	

	Per the International Emmys, the directorate award “is presented to organizations or individuals in management, administration, engineering, news, programming, and/or international relations for outstanding contributions over a period of time to the arts and sciences of international television.”


	Recent winners include Grupo Globo president João Roberto Marinho (2025), Gaumont CEO Sidonie Dumas (2024), Balaji Telefilms’ Ekta Kapoor (2023), CJ ENM’s Miky Lee (2022) and ZDF’s Thomas Bellut (2021).

	Zeiler first joined Time Warner’s Turner in 2012, expanding the company’s international operations, including its regional sports and pay-TV businesses. He was named WarnerMedia International presidnet in 2020, and as president of international for Warner Bros. Discovery, Zeiler has expanded HBO Max footprint to more than 130 countries in just over three years and helped oversee the integration of WarnerMedia and Discovery.
	

	Prior to Turner, he was CEO of RTL, and earlier in his career held senior leadership roles at Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.

	“I am deeply honored to be recognized by the International Academy with the International Emmy Directorate Award,” Zeiler said in a statement. “My passion for media began before I can even remember, and from a young age I understood the power of television to bring people together and open a window into different cultures and ideas. The role of media in connecting the world requires a deep understanding of distinct cultures – global trends and local nuances alike – and I feel very fortunate to have had a career filled with learnings and perspectives across the world on what makes compelling television. This is an industry like no other, driven by passion, ambition, and the desire to create stories that audiences can connect with. I receive this recognition with great appreciation for the colleagues, partners and creative talent who have inspired that journey.”

schema.headline: Warner Bros. Discovery’s Gerhard Zeiler to Recieve Directorate Award at This Year’s International Emmys

title: Stretching Time: Nicolaas Schmidt on ‘September Afternoon’
description: On a windy afternoon, a family packs a beach bag, perhaps for the last time, and languidly walks towards the coast. A sense of gloom hangs in the ai
body:
On a windy afternoon, a family packs a beach bag, perhaps for the last time, and languidly walks towards the coast. A sense of gloom hangs in the air. While the child and her mother play in the sand, the father tackles the seemingly impossible task of setting up a tent to provide shelter. As he begins to fill the bags with sand to weigh down the tent, the wind keeps trumping his efforts, shoveling more sand inside the tent. There’s a sisyphean sensation, emphasized by the instrumental version of a song looped in the background for most of the film.
	

	Following his previous Special Mention for the 2021 title “First Time” at Locarno, Nicolaas Schmidt’s debut feature film “September Afternoon” premiered last week in the Cineasti del Presente section.




	

					Nicolaas Schmidt
									Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival
	



	“September Afternoon,” which begins with footage from a ’90s ice cream commercial and the words “a post-postmodern persistence parable,” adopts the clichéd advertising aesthetic — frontal shots overlaid with music, extreme close-ups set against glistening waves — only to turn it on its head, gradually deforming it into something monumentally strange and unrecognizable. While the film lacks dialogue altogether, elemental gestures are often exaggerated, especially when caused by the wind: At times, the sand lifts in waves, covering the frame in a grainy hue; at others, we hear the sound boom shifting with a thud. 

	The film was shot over just a few days and, although the production had planned for a sunny, nearly windless beach, preparing to generate wind artificially, the weather had other plans. The strong winds not only carry the sensation of discomfort, but also serendipitously become an integral character of the film.
	

	Schmidt alludes to the impossibility and unreliability of language, preferring color and soundtrack to dialogue as a means of conveying various moods. Later in the film, after the separation of the father from the rest of the family, the color red comes to signify a sense of desperation. “I’m not afraid of using clichés.”

	Perhaps what is most compelling about “September Afternoon” is its resistance to narrative time. As in his previous works “Final Stage” (2017) and “First Time” (2021), the accretion of dead time (temps morts) here becomes a guiding principle: What initially appears familiar — the seductive, polished language of the commercial image — begins to resist its own legibility, opening instead onto texture, duration, and sensation.

	This tension is sustained by the film’s movement between the conventions of narrative cinema and the durational logic of video art. Midway through the film, an idyllic walk by the sea, captured in extreme close up, gradually zooms out into a medium shot and finally into a wide shot. Lasting more than 10 minutes, the image begins eviscerated of scale and depth before slowly recovering a figure-ground relationship — from a smudgy surface to be contemplated to an image of a body moving through a landscape. Later, a woman protractedly licks blue ice cream from a cone, her attempts thwarted by ferocious gusts of wind and sand.

	Strewn across the film, such sequences suspend narrative development, allowing images to linger beyond their immediate function. As Schmidt remarks, “I am more interested in experimenting, in getting surprised by an idea … the artistic starting point of a work.” 

	Notwithstanding its pop-inspired aesthetic, there is something almost elemental in Schmidt’s blocks of image and sound, evocative of the earliest days of cinema. It is perhaps fitting, then, that “September Afternoon” includes a clip from Philippe Garrel’s silent and dreamlike avant-garde classic “Le Révélateur,” also centered around a nuclear family. Garrel’s film, a major influence on Schmidt, offers a way to encounter cinema beyond its linear framework: “an in-between state of sleeping and being aware, a fascinating place for cinema to be in.” If “Le Révélateur” revels in highly contrasted blacks and whites, “September Afternoon” finds solace in subtle modulations of grey, of colors either highly saturated or bleached to the point of indiscernibility.
	

	The film’s critique of the commercial image also acquires a distinctly contemporary resonance. Schmidt himself is conscious of how the visual grammar of advertising has migrated into the endlessly curated feeds of social media.

	“Today, it’s less commercials and more social media, stuff like Instagram … problems about fakeness and over-idealization. We all can see it around us. It’s a bit concerning how the world will be, and how the current generation will turn out.”

	In a world saturated with information, where every image is already endlessly recycled and re-appropriated, attention itself becomes a political act.

schema.headline: Stretching Time: Nicolaas Schmidt on ‘September Afternoon’

title: Inside the Disney Machine: How the Iconic Brand Is Discovering the Next Generation of Stars
description: It’s a tale as old as time — or at least the late ’90s. Young actors cut their teeth on Disney youth programming and blossom into fully fledged pop
body:
It’s a tale as old as time — or at least the late ’90s. Young actors cut their teeth on Disney youth programming and blossom into fully fledged pop stars or Academy Award-nominated actors. Some of today’s biggest stars — Zendaya, Selena Gomez, Olivia Rodrigo, and Sabrina Carpenter, for example — got their start in the Disney talent pipeline.

	And a new wave of young megatalent is now ready to take over screens and make their impact on Hollywood at large.
	

	It’s being led by one of Variety‘s Young Hollywood Issue cover stars Malachi Barton; “Descendants: Rise of Red” star Kylie Cantrall; “Camp Rock 3” songstress Liamani Segura; “Percy Jackson” actress Leah Jeffries, to name a few.


	Filling the Disney halls with the next generation of mega-talent was the primary objective Kids & Family president Ayo Davis gave to Charlie Andrews, EVP of live action, and Brenda Kelly Grant, SVP of talent and casting, when they joined forces five years ago. That mission means identifying talent that can not only captivate a new generation of viewers, but also encompass everything it takes to be a star in 2026.

	“Ayo said that priority number one is building the next generation of Disney stars. We all got into a room, and we talked about our best vehicles to do so,” says Andrews. “Brenda and her team have done an unbelievable job of identifying kids not just all across the country, but across the entire world for ‘Descendants,’ ‘Zombies, ‘Cheetah Girls,’ ‘Percy Jackson” and now our new show, ‘Coven Academy‘ coming out soon. It really started with the strategy right away that we need to rebuild that star-making machine that Disney Channel did better than anyone.”
	



	

					“Percy Jackson and the Olympians”
									Disney
	



	Creating the next A-list is a years-long investment that requires finding talent, fostering it, and then keeping that talent in-house as they grow up and begin to seek new opportunities. Disney’s search for fresh faces is now worldwide, across multiple platforms. When they find stars with potential, the interview process begins before the actors are brought in.

	For Grant, it’s one of the best parts of her job — “seeing extraordinary potential before the rest of the world.” Instead of looking at a performance, they’re thinking ahead. “We are looking at who they might become and how we pair them with the right opportunities to support them, to have that belief in them, and to really get them to where they need to be for that dream to come true.”

	She continues, “The audition room just doesn’t tell the whole story anymore. We may be discovering someone through acting, and then we find out later they’re an exceptional singer or songwriter, or they just really have an ability to connect with audiences. The most exciting moments are when someone reveals those dimensions that we didn’t expect.”

	It’s not enough for a young actor today to have good screen presence; they also need to command an audience on social media, the latter of which brings fresh eyes to Disney content. Talent are then able to have a direct relationship with fans who will also buy merch, concert tickets and attend events.

	“We are entering a new era of Disney stardom because the combination of streaming music, live experiences, and the way we can pair them together just builds these deeper relationships with the talent,” Kelly Grant says. “That’s what this generation does best. They’re not in one lane — they’re trying all of these different things. The definition of a star has really evolved, and our talent are meeting audiences where they are.”



	

					Milo Manheim and Meg Donnelly in “Zombies”
									Disney/Matt Klitscher
	



	Andrews says the company has a symbiotic relationship with TikTok and other social media platforms. Social strategy was integral in Milo Manheim and Meg Donnelly passing the “Zombies” baton to Barton and Freya Skye, for example. It also helped make the “Worlds Collide” live concert tour a record-breaking success.

	“You saw all these young kids going to that concert, oftentimes the first concert of their entire lives. They or their parents are filming those moments; it goes viral, and it felt like a can’t-miss event,” he explains. “That live experience started with the movie, went to the concert, and was only amplified by these kids posting very real moments of themselves. Then it felt can’t-miss for everyone else out there, so they had to go buy tickets themselves.”
	

	The executives cannot lose sight of the fact that they are working with minors. There are numerous resources within the Disney ecosystem, including on-set psychologists and therapists to help talent navigate any issues they may face, online or off. Kelly Grant and Andrews also maintain close relationships with talent even after they’ve been cast in a project.

	“We try to have a very big presence on these sets, making sure we are having our lunches, coffees, and dinners with them, even in between projects, so that we’re having constant check-ins. So then we know what they’re thinking, how they’re doing, and what they need,” Andrews says. “I believe they feel that direct line to us, so that if anything does come up, they feel safe in having that conversation on anything they might need.”


	Acting and singing have always seemed like prerequisites for Disney talent, but those demands are even more intense in the TikTok era. Kelly Grant and Andrews make sure they’re making the most of those talents by casting and creating roles that allow their young stars to stretch their wings.

	Once talent sign with Disney, they have access to the Becoming program, providing extra training in acting, singing, dancing, and various other performance arts so they can become all-around talent. Kids & Family also has a strong relationship with The Music Group, so their stars can continue working on music while filming a show or film.

	“What’s incredible about these kids is that they are actors. They are performers. They are dancers. They are singers. And they are all content creators on top of that. They are creating things online and in our content that speaks directly to the audience,” says Andrews. “Not everyone is the same. A really big role for us is to make sure we acknowledge all facets of them.”

	When that talent is developed, Disney doesn’t want to lose it to other studios or platforms. Luckily, the company is large enough to cover the entire entertainment spectrum, which means as talent ages, they still remain Team Mickey Mouse. Manheim grew up on the Disney Channel and helped turn “Zombies” into a flagship franchise for Kids & Family. Next, he’ll star as Flynn Rider in Disney Studios’ live-action adaptation of “Tangled.” However, he and Donnelly remain producers of the franchise.



	

					Selena Gomez and Jennifer Stone in “Wizards Beyond Waverly Place”
									Disney
	



	Selena Gomez returned to the Disney family in 2021 to star in Hulu’s “Only Murders in the Building,” which made it easier to bring her back to Kids & Family as a producer and star of “Wizards Beyond Waverly Place.” Kelly Grant and Andrews leverage Disney’s portfolio of platforms to give the talent they are developing more grown-up opportunities while keeping them in-house.
	

	Barton will continue in the “Zombies” franchise, but will also star in the upcoming “Coven Academy” from “High School Musical: The Musical: The Series” creator Tim Federle. “Coven” caters more squarely to a teen audience than Disney Channel fare and will help its cast age with their fans now teenagers and entering young adulthood. The series will debut on Freeform on Oct. 1; the next day, the full season will be available to stream on Disney+, Hulu and Freeform on Demand.

	“I love the ecosystem that Disney can offer. We have performers that move from a series to a film, to music and concerts, and continue to grow creatively while staying connected to their audience,” says Kelly Grant. “That’s what makes us different.”

	Andrews adds, “We are thinking about roles on the movies side for them, and with our family content, but also Hulu and FX. We want the audience to age with them but stay on our platforms. We want to find those roles for them so they start as part of the Disney family at all times.”

	Creating the next-generation superstar is understanding what a star actually means in the modern day. Disney believes it has that figured out and is helping its talent meet those demands and take over Hollywood.

	“People say that there’s not a traditional movie star anymore, but I think the definition has just expanded. Today’s stars are not just confined to one screen or one platform,” Kelly Grant declares. “When I look at the talent coming through right now, that’s very exciting to me. We’re looking at the next generation of performers and how they will define the future.”

description: Is there an audience for AI-delivered news? Public data says no, and previous attempts to deliver such ventures have yielded many human-written stor
body:
Is there an audience for AI-delivered news? Public data says no, and previous attempts to deliver such ventures have yielded many human-written stories about projects that never materialized.

	And yet Mirage — the AI startup behind the video-editing app Captions that raised $75 million this year and was last valued at $500 million — thinks someone, somewhere out there may have a hunger for an AI avatar to supplant their cable news habits but just hasn’t had an outlet to indulge in it.
	

	Enter the “Mirage News Network,” the company’s roughly $50,000 daylong experiment this week to create a 24-hour newscast where AI-generated news anchors cover real stories. The Tuesday broadcast reached a total of 50,000 viewers on X, with its livestream post reaching 824,000 impressions and drawing responses ranging from curious to captious — while Mirage paid several accounts, including @historyinmemes, to promote the livestream.


	The four anchors were completely generated by an AI agent using a mixture of Mirage’s Avatar X model, which the Mirage News Network release was ostensibly launched to promote, and tools like ChatGPT’s image generator and Google’s Gemini Text-to-Speech feature. The days-old stories were licensed from Reuters’ wire service, and the only real people to appear across the stream were those featured in the videos that Reuters journalists filmed and the stock footage that accompanied such packages. For AI-generated guests who appeared for “interviews,” Mirage recruited more than a dozen people, mostly venture capital professionals, who authorized their likenesses and approved the scripts for what their likenesses would say. (One notable name: Billy McFarland, of Fyre Festival and federal prison fame.)
	

	Mirage CEO Gaurav Misra, who built and managed the project by himself with $30,000 worth of Claude Code, wanted the newscast to feel like a traditional broadcast, drawing inspiration from ’80s-style newscasters’ looks and appearances with names like “Tom Callahan” and “Marcus Sterling.” His mission, Misra told Variety, was to figure out whether there was an appetite for something that resembled the news but where nothing but the stories themselves was rooted in reality.

	“The goal of this was not exactly to be the news or to fool anybody, or to pretend to look real,” he said. “In fact, the goal was to make sure that people know that this is AI-generated. That was the most important part.”

	Yet Jason Silberman, a software engineer at Mirage, may have given away the game in an X post: “when the CEO starts tokenmaxxing too hard and spends $50k in a day on a marketing stunt.” “Tokenmaxxing,” according to one definition, refers to “maximizing AI token usage — and treating that volume as proof of productivity.”

	Still, Misra’s points touch on a foundational element of ethical journalism, which the Society of Professional Journalists’ code of ethics demands be “accountable and transparent” in the work. But such codes did not power the Mirage project — nor did any journalists who would adhere to such rules, because no journalists work at the company and it is not a news organization. 

	Misra’s background is not in news but in tech, having worked as a software engineer at Snap and Microsoft. His instructions to the machine were not to follow any specific ethical code, guidelines or style, such as the journalistic bible of AP style or the widely accepted SPJ Code of Ethics, but instead to adhere to “general journalistic standards,” Misra said. The product represents another example in the AI era of a group of people — in this case, fewer than 10 — working on a project within a specific industry without a perspective informed by years of experience in that field.

	On one hand, the operation was transparent. The livestream featured a graphic in the top-left corner signifying nearly everything on the screen — the anchors reading the story scripts, the graphics accompanying such stories, the “guests” who appeared for interviews and even the commercials between segments  — was artificially created. When the program made errors — and it did, repeatedly, such as incorrectly identifying a woman in a Reuters package as President Donald Trump — the company disclosed such errors on its X account. (Though it did not, as most TV news outlets do, do that during the broadcast itself; Misra watched the livestream hours ahead of the broadcast to try and catch errors before they aired.)
	

	But such a lack of experience in news or specificity in journalistic standards in working on a project like this on an experiment such as this represents “a false and misguided devaluing and deskilling of journalism,” said Dan Axelrod, a former journalist who currently chairs the SPJ’s ethics committee, who called the endeavor not a news network but “a news delivery project” that was not “creating a product that adds value to the marketplace.” The SPJ ethics committee this week introduced a draft revision of its code for the AI age, designed to press journalists to adhere to their ethical obligations as technology adapts. 

	“Nobody says, ‘Let me go do my own surgery,’” Axelrod said. “Few people say, and many immediately come to regret it, ‘Let me defend myself in court.’ Everybody thinks they can communicate, or be the best communicator, or be the best storyteller, and they don’t take into account all of the training and all of the experiential learning and all of the ethical guidance that a high-level professional journalist follows, and they don’t take into account or value [it].”

	Axelrod said the project betrayed journalistic credibility because such work “hinges on the simple promise that a human with professional judgment stands behind the story, and the news unites in that it captures and connects us by our humanity.” 

	“We watch it to see and feel the things that other humans see and feel,” Axelrod added, “and that goes for the journalists, not just the people covered in the stories.”

	News was the first industry Mirage tackled because he didn’t believe it could be replicated through AI. But now that the company has produced this, Misra thinks there’s a world where AI-generated newscasts are “probably inevitable in the future” bcause AI “seems to be surprisingly good at just stating the facts, stating the facts in a way that doesn’t even try to hint towards which one is the right answer, which is which is not easy, or at least it seems to be not easy.”

	Misra’s belief in how journalism should be delivered hinges somewhere along recognizing “a battle between being completely dry and accurate versus actually something that people want to watch” while believing people opting for opinion-based content that was “more entertaining, probably.” His news diet consists of small bits of TV news, Google News aggregations and for “the rest of it, I depend on TikTok.”
	

	But Misra believes there may be an audience for such endeavors, “everyday people” who he thinks may prefer a generated person to a living, breathing anchor for “a different angle” for news. It also, he contended, “just lowers the barrier for more people to be able to participate in in creating content and things like that.”

	“But I don’t think it’s necessarily true that you know people want one thing or the other,” he said. “I think different people might be happy with different things.”

	Public data suggests otherwise. 

	According to a Gallup survey conducted in May 2026, only 7% of Americans either rely “a great deal” (2%) or “a fair amount” (5%) on AI to get news, but nearly 40% of Americans polled believe that a news organization’s use of AI would “reduce my trust in the information.” Similar figures were produced by the Pew Research Center last year regarding AI chatbots, with nearly 60% of adults between ages 18 to 29 and 51% of adults between 30 and 49 believing at least some of the news produced by chatbots is inaccurate. In June, Pew found that 40% of respondents believe AI would ultimately be worse for society.

	It raises a question that only “Stephanie Kwan,” the “tech desk” “reporter” for the “Mirage News Network” could pose, as the AI avatar did for a Reuters package about robot dogs replacing security guards in Atlanta.

	“So why swap out the humans?”

body:
Christy Knowings, who was a cast member on Nickelodeon’s children sketch comedy show “All That,” died Tuesday. She was 46.

	Knowings suffered an asthma attack that left her with brain damage, according to TMZ, and she was hospitalized on Friday. TMZ, which broke the news of Knowings’ death, reported that she was placed on life support in Los Angeles and was removed on Tuesday night. Her aunt, Tyleah Joseph, announced Knowings’ death on Wednesday on Facebook.
	

	“Christy was a multi-talented lady. Whether it was singing, acting, dancing, she was always creating. Always professional and dedicated to her work,” her manager Al Hill said in a statement to Variety.


	Knowings was a main cast member on “All That” for three season between 1997 and 2001, and she rejoined as a guest star in Season 10. She joined the cast alongside Leon Frierson and Danny Tamborelli for Season 4 after being first discovered on the pilot for a Rosie O’Donnell-produced sketch show called “And Now This.” The trio of “All That” newcomers crossed over with original series stars like Amanda Bynes, Kenan Thompson, Kel Mitchell, Lori Beth Denberg and Josh Server. During their run, the show later added comedians like Nick Cannon and Gabriel Iglesias to their ranks.

	“Man this one hit hard!!!,” Thompson wrote on Facebook. “Rest well Christy!!! Never could have imagined this day!! Sending so much love to her family!! She was a real one and one of the funniest people out here!!! Gonna miss you buddy!!! Show christyknowings ★ some love y’all!!!”

	Outside of “All That,” Knowings also appeared on three episodes of “Sesame Street” along with her twin brother, Chris — who was a fellow member of Nickelodeon shows like “Taina” and “The Nick Cannon Show.” After acting on “All That,” Knowings took a step back from Hollywood but released a folk music single in 2020 titled “To the World.”

title: Xzibit Says He and Ex-Wife Have Settled Child Support and Custody Issues
description:
Xzibit to Judge
                          We're On Same Page About Our Kid ...
body:
Xzibit to Judge
                          We're On Same Page About Our Kid ...
                          But My Ex Should Still Be Punished
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            12:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Xzibit says he and his ex-wife have finally come to an agreement on issues involving property and their child ... meaning their years-long legal drama may soon be finalized ... but he's still got an axe to grind over how she and her lawyer handled the case ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The rapper filed a document earlier this month ... and checked off boxes indicating he and Krista Joiner have come to an agreement regarding property issues, child custody and visitation, and child support. The former couple share a son, Gatlyn, who was born in 2010.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Despite reaching a deal on these issues, Xzibit also filed documents claiming he's spent $1.6 million in attorneys' fees and costs over the last five years litigating the case ... which includes around $400K in attorneys' fees he says he's paid for Krista's lawyers. He claims Krista and her lawyer engaged in "scorched earth tactics" that delayed settlement and ran up the costs of the case
      

            Xzibit's asking a judge to hit Krista with at least $200K in sanctions to punish her for how she litigated the case, which he believes was an effort to "wreak havoc, harass, and intimidate" him.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We broke the story ... Xzibit's wife filed for divorce way back in 2021 -- the two had reportedly been together for two decades up to that point, though they were only married for about 6 years.
      
    
            Fast forward to 2025 ... when Xzibit filed docs asking the judge to declare him legally single while the estranged couple hashed out property, custody, and other issues.
      
    
            The court granted his request -- and now it looks like the Xzibit and Krista worked out the remaining issues to finally put the marriage behind them.

title: Parents of Baby Born By Surrogate McKenna West Against Their Wishes Have Custody of Child For Now
description:
Surrogacy Drama
                          Biological Parents Have Custody of Child For Now
body:
Surrogacy Drama
                          Biological Parents Have Custody of Child For Now
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            10:33 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 13, 2026
                                1:16 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The biological parents of the baby born to a surrogate who refused to have an abortion against their wishes have custody of the child for now ... at least according to their lawyer, who says the political theater surrounding the birth "devastated" them.
      
    
            Lee Budner of Calabrese Budner, counsel to the baby's biological parents, tells TMZ ... their son -- named Gabriel by surrogate McKenna West -- was born Wednesday morning and is now in their physical custody while he receives medical care.
      
    
            The couple's lawyer adds ... his clients are placing the baby's health first and following the advice of his medical team.
      

            Budner says, "As if the heartbreak of his condition were not enough, they are devastated to see their family tragedy transformed into political theater by the Texas Attorney General's office and McKenna West."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Budner finishes the statement by making it clear the parents' top priority is spending as much time as possible with their child while also ensuring the kid gets the medical care he vitally needs.
      
    
            As you know ... doctors discovered the fetus was suffering from a hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) -- a rare birth defect where the left side of the heart does not grow correctly -- during the 20-week scan.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The birth agreement included a clause where the biological parents could choose to terminate the pregnancy if an "anomaly" was found ... but West ran off with the child instead -- fleeing to Texas, where she hoped she would be seen as the birth mother, The Dallas Morning News reports.
      
    
            She was due to give birth September 2 ... but the baby was born early. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton obtained an emergency court order requiring two Dallas hospitals -- UT Southwestern Medical Center and Children's Medical Center of Dallas -- to provide life-saving care to the baby, according to reports.
      
    
            Story developing ...

title: Surrogate Who Refused to Terminate Pregnancy Despite Intended Parents Wishes Gives Birth
description:
Surrogacy Drama
                          Woman Who Refused to Abort Baby Gives Birth
body:
Surrogacy Drama
                          Woman Who Refused to Abort Baby Gives Birth
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            6:04 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 13, 2026
                                1:26 PM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
          Update
  
    
            1:12 PM PT -- McKenna West will have no authority over the baby according to legal docs obtained by TMZ.
      
    
            10:33 AM PT -- The biological parents of the newborn baby born into surrogacy who refused to have an abortion against their wishes, now have temporary custody of their child.
      
    
            A surrogate who refused to abort the baby she was carrying -- despite the wishes of the boy’s biological parents -- reportedly gave birth early Wednesday amid a bitter legal battle with the intended parents.
      
    
            Here's the sitch -- McKenna West, a surrogate from Alaska, was carrying a baby for a California couple. At the fetus' 20-week scan, doctors discovered it had hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS), a rare birth defect where the left side of the heart does not grow correctly ... and it needs 3 surgeries to correct when the child is born, per Boston Children's Hospital.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The surrogacy agreement had a clause that allowed the couple to choose to terminate the pregnancy if there was an "anomaly" found ... but McKenna refused and fled to Texas, where she would be seen as the birth mother, The Dallas Morning News reports.
      

            She was due to give birth Sept. 2, but delivered the boy -- baby Gabriel -- Wednesday in the Dallas area, her attorney, Lincoln Wilson, told Dallas Morning News.
      
    
            The attorney for the intended parents, Lee Budner, told the outlet ... "Our clients' only focus at this time is ensuring that their baby receives the medical care that he vitally needs and that they, as his parents, are able to spend every precious moment they can with him."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The intended parents are suing McKenna and had a court date later this month. It's unclear how this unique multi-state legal battle will play out ... at this point, McKenna is not allowed to see or care for Gabriel, but her attorney said she's considered taking the child if the court rules she can.
      
    
            Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton obtained an emergency court order requiring two Dallas hospitals -- UT Southwestern Medical Center and Children's Medical Center of Dallas -- to provide life-saving care to the baby, according to reports.
      
    
            Meanwhile, McKenna's lawyer reportedly said the termination clause within the surrogacy contract she signed is "offensive to state and federal law."
      
    
            Before she gave birth, McKenna told Live Action she simply believed Gabriel deserved a chance at life.

            12:13 PM PT -- Kenan Thompson took to Instagram to pay tribute to his his fellow "All That" star.
      
    
            Former "All That" star Christy Knowings is dead after suffering an asthma attack that left her with brain damage ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            A family member tells TMZ ... Christy was hospitalized Friday after the attack and placed on life support.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told Christy remained on life support through Tuesday, when her family made the difficult decision to take her off it. She died Tuesday night at a Los Angeles-area hospital.
      

            The actress and comedian joined Nickelodeon's "All That" in 1997 after appearing in "And Now This" -- a Rosie O'Donnell sketch-comedy special produced by the network.
      
    
            Christy spent three seasons on "All That" playing several characters, including Penny Lane and Jessica on the recurring "Whateverrr!!!" sketch with Amanda Bynes.
      
    
            She later appeared in 3 episodes of "Sesame Street" alongside her real-life twin brother, Chris Knowings ... and released the folk single "To the World" in 2020.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Christy is the second former "All That" cast member to die this year. As TMZ previously reported ... Kianna Underwood was killed in a hit-and-run collision in Brooklyn in January.
      
    
            Christy was 46.

title: Ex-Porn Star Jenna Jameson's Marriage to Jessica Lawless Annulled Before 4th Wedding
description:
Ex-Porn Star Jenna Jameson
                          Ex-Wife Annulled Marriage Year Before Her 4t
body:
Ex-Porn Star Jenna Jameson
                          Ex-Wife Annulled Marriage Year Before Her 4th Wedding
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            12:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Jenna Jameson's ex, Jessica Lawless, successfully annulled their marriage roughly a year before the former porn star walked down the aisle for the fourth time ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Jessica filed a petition to annul their marriage in 2025. Jenna failed to respond, and a judge entered a decree of annulment on April 14, 2025, restoring both women to unmarried status.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Jessica initially filed for an annulment in 2024, claiming Jenna entered into the marriage under false pretenses -- but that case was dismissed. Jenna later filed her own divorce case, though it appears that case went nowhere.
      

            In the OG annulment filing, Jessica claimed Jenna lied about being debt-free when they tied the knot in 2023 ... and also claimed Jenna said she was sober when, according to Jessica, she wasn't.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            As TMZ first reported, Jenna recently married Milagros Ocampo in Miami, marking her fourth trip down the aisle.
